(3) Double counting: where two projects' sampling frames overlap, pool only surveys whose frames partition the domain, or re-derive the design weights for the combined sample; where neither is possible, report the project values separately. Named overlap: the grain counted here is also part of the total staple grain in per-capita staple food availability (KPI-OC13), so the two must never be added together.
eligibilityCriteriaMissingData: Inclusion: all biofortified grain available in the intervention area, including grain traded in from outside; grain that arrived through the market is as available as grain grown locally, and the locally produced share is reported alongside, because the two carry different implications for what CIMMYT should do next. The grain must be of varieties whose claim for a named target nutrient or trait meets the evidence standard in KPI-O07's Eligibility criteria and missing data, whatever its origin, including farmer-saved seed of such varieties.
limitations: Availability is not intake and not nutritional status. The grain may be eaten by people who were not deficient, sold on, or fed to animals, and the micronutrient still has to be absorbed. Any micronutrient-adequacy claim is inferential, and CGIAR's own review of its standard indicators notes that "minimum micronutrient requirements" is not yet defined for reporting, so no conversion from kilograms to people meeting requirements exists.

Variety identification is the main measurement error. Biofortified grain looks like conventional grain of the same crop, so farmer-reported variety names misclassify in both directions, and micronutrient concentration varies with soil, agronomy, seed recycling, and processing, which milling in particular can strip out.

Sub-national availability accounting is not standard practice. National food balance sheets, the recognised source for per-capita availability, do not resolve a project area, so values rest on local survey accounting whose assumptions about seed, feed, losses, and grain crossing the boundary drive the result as much as the harvest does.

Supports a contribution claim only. Availability also moves with rainfall, prices, market access, and other organisations' seed programmes, and the denominator shifts with migration in and out of the area, so the value can change with no change in CIMMYT's work.

A rise means more biofortified grain was available per person than at baseline. It does not mean people ate it, that diets improved, or that CIMMYT caused the change; pair it with the adoption share (KPI-OC10) and dietary or food-security evidence for the contribution narrative.
subMetrics: None. The numerator components (harvest, inflows, stock changes, seed, feed, post-harvest loss, outflows) are calculation terms, not separately reported metrics. Related sheets in the same results chain: KPI-O06, KPI-O07 and KPI-O09 (biofortified or nutrient-dense varieties disseminated, released, and made available), KPI-OC10 (share of target farmers cultivating them), KPI-OC13 (per-capita staple food availability), and KPI-I02 (prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity), the impact indicator this outcome group rolls up to.
referenceStandardsAndLinks: Every other source is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports; the reference list is at the end of this volume.
sheetStewardDataRoles: Data collection: project M&E team and enumerators (production and utilisation module, variety identification). Validation: project MEAL officer (component completeness, variety identification, weighting). Calculation: project M&E, per the Calculation method above. Approval: project leader. Reporting: project MEAL focal point to the CIMMYT MEAL unit.
sourceRef: Volume 3 · Nutrition & food security — Reference sheet KPI-OC08

name: Share of households in CIMMYT intervention areas able to afford a healthy diet, based on the FAO Cost and Affordability of a Healthy Diet (CoAHD) methodology
resultsLevel: Outcome (a change in the economic condition of households reached; feeds the pathway's impact-level food-security indicators through the theory of change)
primaryObjective: PO2 Food and nutrition security in the global south is ensured within planetary boundaries. Contributing objective: PO3 Smallholder farmers and their livelihood trajectories are resilient and significantly improved.
cgiarImpactArea: Nutrition, Health & Food Security, following what the indicator measures, per the pathway-wide rule.
sdgTarget: None. CoAHD is not part of the official SDG indicator framework. FAO positions the indicators as supporting SDG 2 (end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition); the closest official SDG indicators, 2.1.1 (undernourishment) and 2.1.2 (FIES), are separate constructs covered by their own reference sheets.
otherFrameworks: FAO and World Bank joint CoAHD monitoring, published annually in The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World (FAO, IFAD, UNICEF, WFP, WHO) and in the five Regional Overviews of Food Security and Nutrition; full data series on the FAOSTAT CoAHD domain.
definition: Measures the percentage of households in CIMMYT intervention areas whose income is sufficient to purchase a healthy diet for all household members. Affordability is assessed with the FAO Cost and Affordability of a Healthy Diet (CoAHD) methodology, which compares the cost of the least expensive locally available diet meeting national dietary guideline requirements against the income a household has for food. The sheet uses FAO's term "healthy diet", as the register title now does; the register's Definition cell still reads "nutritious diet". The numerator, the denominator and the construction of the diet cost are in Calculation method. FAO writes the methodology CoAHD and the FAOSTAT data domain CAHD; both name the same construct.
rationale: Answers whether CIMMYT's agrifood systems work translates into economic access to healthy diets for households in its intervention areas: unaffordability of healthy diets is one of the key drivers of food insecurity and malnutrition that CIMMYT's 2030 Strategy targets. Because CoAHD is the FAO and World Bank global standard, reported annually for 173 countries, values are anchored to an internationally recognised method and speak directly to institutional and donor reporting on nutrition and food security.
projectSpecificApplication: State the intervention area the affordability test is applied in, the local price set used for the HDB food groups, and the survey rounds the income or consumption-expenditure measure comes from. If applying the indicator as defined is not feasible in this project's context, raise it with the MEAL focal point rather than redefining it here. Example: the cost of the least-cost healthy diet priced from local retail food prices across the HDB food groups, compared against household income or total consumption expenditure measured in the project's own household survey at baseline and endline. The institutional definition, the HDB standard, and the affordability test are unchanged; only the population, the local price set, and the survey timing are project-specific. Record that FAO's published national figures are computed at the individual level from national income distributions; the project-level household share is a local application of the same method, not a re-estimate of the national statistic.
projectSpecificRationale: State the project decision or donor requirement this value informs. Example: showing whether productivity gains, income gains or lower food prices through improved supply move households toward economic access to a healthy diet; a stagnant share alongside rising production or income signals that food price or market barriers need attention in adaptive management.
projectTypesNotApplicable: whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no household population whose income and local food prices could be surveyed
projectTypesRaw:
Breeding and varietal development; applied agronomy and farming systems; seed systems and deployment; system change and transformation; digital agriculture and AI.

Not applicable: upstream discovery science, whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no household population whose income and local food prices could be surveyed.
unit: Percentage of households
directionOfChange: Increase. A rising value means a larger share of households can afford a healthy diet. Record the sign convention: FAO publishes the prevalence of people unable to afford one, which moves in the opposite direction, so the national series, used only for comparison, is read as 100 minus that figure and sits at individual rather than household resolution.
disaggregationRequired: Sex of household head (male/female at minimum, per the register's own disaggregation rule; no CGIAR sex-disaggregation standard is named in this sheet or in the sources consulted, so none is cited for it).
disaggregationRequiredForProjectType: None. The register names a project type in none of its rows, so no cut is required by project type; the cuts above apply to every type that reports this indicator.
disaggregationProjectSpecific: Rural/urban, agroecological zone, income quintile, gendered household type.
unitOfObservation: Household
calculationSummary:
A household is counted as able to afford a healthy diet when its income available for food is at least the cost of the least-cost healthy diet for all its members. The affordability test is income net of a basic-needs allowance, FAO's current poverty-line-based approach: total income, or total consumption expenditure where the survey measures that instead, minus the cost of basic non-food needs for all members, each member's allowance being the World Bank international poverty line for the country's income group multiplied by the non-food expenditure share of people near the poverty line, as applied in the FAOSTAT release in force and converted to local currency at the price date, so CIMMYT's values sit on the same basis as the published FAOSTAT series; a project may report an alternative test alongside where it has the data, but never instead. The diet cost follows the FAO method, operationalised through the Healthy Diet Basket: for each of the six HDB food groups (starchy staples; vegetables; fruits; animal source foods; legumes, nuts and seeds; oils and fats) every locally available item priced in that group is costed per kilocalorie, the least expensive items are selected in the number the basket sets for the group (two starchy staples, three vegetables, two fruits, two animal source foods, one legume, nut or seed, and one oil or fat, eleven items in all), each is costed at an equal share of the group's energy target (totalling 2,330 kcal per person per day), and the group costs are summed. A diet is unaffordable when its cost exceeds the income remaining once basic non-food needs are covered. The household diet cost is scaled per capita, matching FAO's per person per day basis for the 2,330 kcal reference intake; adult equivalence would change the denominator away from FAO's and take the diet cost off FAO's per person basis.

Numerator: surveyed households whose income available for food covers the household's healthy diet cost. Denominator: all surveyed households in the intervention area. Value = (numerator / denominator) x 100, applying survey weights. Every inclusion, exclusion, missing-data and repeated-observation rule is in Eligibility criteria and missing data; none is restated here.
dataSource: Recommended DS1: project household survey with an income or consumption-expenditure module, paired with a local market price survey covering the locally available items in each HDB food group, from which the eleven least-cost items are selected, both collected in the project's intervention area. Comparator DS4: the FAOSTAT CoAHD national series (prevalence of unaffordability, read as 100 minus PUA), used to place the project's household share against the national individual-level figure; never a substitute for the project survey, never pooled, and never reported as a KPI-OC09 value. Where the project cannot field its own survey, the indicator is recorded as not reportable for that project and period. Not applicable: DS2 and DS3. Affordability compares household income against a locally priced diet; neither side can be read from administrative records or Earth observation. DS5 is also not applicable: crowdsourced data cannot supply the household income side of the affordability test.
dataSourceProjectSpecific: Name the household survey and the local market price survey the value was computed from, with their windows. Example: "The project's own baseline and endline household survey plus its local market price survey."
collectionInstrument: Household survey income or consumption-expenditure module (adapted from the national LSMS-type instrument in use in the project country), plus the standard market price module: CIMMYT MEAL develops one standard market price module for the Healthy Diet Basket items, rather than leaving each project to build its own, since FAO publishes no project-level field instrument and prices collected on different baskets, in different market types, on different days are not comparable between projects. The module specifies the item list, the market type and the collection window. Respondent: household head or the adult most knowledgeable about household finances. Mode: face-to-face interview; market prices collected by enumerators at typical retail outlets following the module's standardised protocol (consistent item specification, quantity, and outlet type across waves).
collectionFrequency: Baseline and endline; for multi-year programmes, a midline every 2 to 3 years. Local price collection accompanies each survey wave.
reportingFrequency: Annually; between measurement waves the latest measured value is carried forward with its year of measurement noted.
referencePeriod: The survey round year: household income over the survey recall period, compared against local food prices collected in the same window (FAO practice uses annual average prices; where the project collects prices in one season, the season is stated with the value). Change is assessed against the pre-intervention baseline.
baselineRequired: Yes. Where no prospective baseline exists: secondary pre-period household survey data for the area, if available. If none is feasible: monitoring only, no change or impact claims.
aggregationRule:
A: Pooling domain. (2) Aggregation across projects: pool household data directly.

B: Combination method. Pool at household level using survey weights: the institutional figure is the weighted share of households able to afford a healthy diet across all projects that report a value. Never average project-level percentages.

C: Levels and operations. A share is recomputed at every level from its own numerator and denominator, never averaged from the levels beneath it: a mean of project percentages weights a project of three hundred households equally with one of three thousand. At Household, the affordability test is applied to that household's income available for food against the cost of the least-cost healthy diet for its own members; no share is reported at that level. At project level, households passing the test over all households with complete income or expenditure data, applying survey weights. At Regional / Aggregated and institutional level, the summed weighted numerator over the summed weighted denominator within the pooling domain of Block A, computed from household records rather than from project shares. Also report: the denominator; the number of households excluded for an incomplete module; the cost of a healthy diet itself in local currency alongside the share, since a share that moved cannot be read without knowing whether prices or incomes moved; the season and window in which prices were collected; and whether the test used total income or total consumption expenditure.

D: Never pooled. (1) Aggregation across results levels: no. This outcome value is never added to output-level or impact-level values in the Nutrition & food security pathway; it connects to the pathway's impact indicators (food-insecurity prevalence) through the theory of change as a narrative, not through arithmetic. Overlap with other register indicators: this indicator draws on the same household surveys as the food-insecurity (FIES) indicator but measures a different construct, economic access rather than experienced insecurity; report both, and never sum or substitute one for the other.

E: Deduplication and coverage. (3) Double counting: where two projects' sampling frames overlap, pool only surveys whose frames partition the domain, or re-derive the design weights for the combined sample; where neither is possible, report the project values separately.
eligibilityCriteriaMissingData: Include sampled households in the project's intervention area with a complete income or consumption-expenditure module, tested against local food price data collected in the same survey window. Exclude households whose income or expenditure module is incomplete, and any period for which no local price data exist. Missing data: an excluded household leaves the denominator rather than being imputed; a missing price for an HDB food group is filled from the nearest comparable market in the same survey window and the fill is flagged with the value. Repeated observations: where a household is re-contacted within the same survey round, only the first completed interview counts and later duplicates are dropped.
limitations: Supports a contribution claim only: diet affordability moves with food prices, wages, non-farm income, social protection, and macroeconomic conditions; CIMMYT's interventions are one contributor among many. Pair with adoption, productivity, and income indicators for the contribution narrative.

The affordability test is assumption-sensitive: results shift with how income is measured and how the non-food basic-needs allowance is set. FAO itself revises the CoAHD series backward as methods improve, so values must come from a consistent method across waves, and project figures must not be compared against FAO figures from different report editions.

Project household shares are not directly comparable to FAO's published national values: FAO computes prevalence among individuals from national income distributions and ICP (International Comparison Program) prices, while this indicator counts households against locally collected prices.

The least-cost healthy diet is a lower bound: real diets cost more because of preferences, time, and market access. A household counted as "able to afford" is not necessarily consuming a healthy diet, so an improvement means economic access widened, not that diets improved; read alongside the volume's dietary energy adequacy (KPI-OC07) and food-insecurity (KPI-I02) indicators.
Local price collection is a major error source: item specification, outlet choice, and seasonal timing all move the diet cost, so the price protocol must stay constant across waves.
referenceStandardsAndLinks: Every other source is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports; the reference list is at the end of this volume.
sheetStewardDataRoles: Data collection: project M&E team / enumerators (household survey and market price survey). Validation: project MEAL officer. Calculation: CIMMYT MEAL unit (per Calculation method above). Approval: project team lead. Reporting: project MEAL focal point to the CIMMYT MEAL unit.

name: Share of target farmers cultivating officially released biofortified or nutrient-dense varieties containing CIMMYT-derived germplasm
resultsLevel: Outcome. What is measured is what farmers choose to plant, a change in practice among beneficiaries, which is the Core's definition of an outcome. CGIAR's quality assurance guidance uses farmers using a new seed variety as its own example of an outcome. The upstream steps are counted separately at output level: varieties released, an act of the national or regional authority to which CIMMYT contributes germplasm (KPI-O07), and varieties disseminated by CIMMYT and its delivery partners (KPI-O06).
primaryObjective: PO2 Food and nutrition security in the global south is ensured within planetary boundaries. Contributing: PO3 (Smallholder farmers and their livelihood trajectories are resilient and significantly improved).
cgiarImpactArea: Nutrition, Health & Food Security
sdgTarget: None. No SDG indicator measures adoption of biofortified varieties. The indicator serves target 2.2 (by 2030, end all forms of malnutrition, including addressing the nutritional needs of adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women and older persons), but that target is monitored at nutritional-status level by indicators 2.2.1 to 2.2.3 (child stunting, child wasting and overweight, anaemia in women aged 15 to 49), which measure people's condition, not what farmers plant.
otherFrameworks: CGIAR's results framework tracks the number of people meeting minimum micronutrient requirements at impact level; adoption of biofortified varieties is a contributing pathway to that result, not a measure of it.
definition: Measures the percentage of farmers in a project's target population who grew at least one officially released biofortified or nutrient-dense variety containing CIMMYT-derived germplasm, on land they manage themselves, during the cropping seasons of the reporting year. Release is the act of the competent national or regional authority; CIMMYT's contribution is the germplasm. The target population is the farmers the project registered or reached. Biofortified or nutrient-dense covers micronutrient biofortification (provitamin A, zinc, iron) and protein quality, including quality protein maize, recorded with the target nutrient or trait named, not yield or stress tolerance alone. The eligible varieties and the ancestry rule are in Eligibility criteria and missing data.
rationale: Answers whether the officially released biofortified varieties built on CIMMYT germplasm are being grown by the farmers the work is aimed at. Contributing germplasm to a release and distributing the seed says nothing about uptake, while grain availability and household food security sit further downstream and move with prices, weather and much else. This is the first point in the biofortification chain at which someone outside CIMMYT has changed what they do, so project management, institutional reporting and donors need it in order to read the later results.
projectSpecificApplication: State the crops, countries, districts and cropping seasons covered, which farmers make up the target population, and how the project establishes that a variety on a farmer's plot is an eligible CIMMYT release. Do not change the unit, the numerator and denominator, or the counting rules. If the target population cannot be enumerated well enough to form a denominator, raise it with the MEAL focal point rather than redefining the indicator here.
projectSpecificRationale: State the project decision or donor requirement this value serves. It is also an adaptive-management trigger: high awareness of a biofortified variety with a low cultivation share points to a seed supply, price or grain-market problem rather than to weak farmer interest, and calls for a different response than low awareness would.
projectTypesNotApplicable: whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no target farmer population whose planting decisions could be observed
projectTypesRaw:
Breeding and varietal development; applied agronomy and farming systems; seed systems and deployment; system change and transformation; digital agriculture and AI.

Not applicable: upstream discovery science, whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no target farmer population whose planting decisions could be observed.
unit: Percentage of target farmers
directionOfChange: Increase. A rising value means a larger share of target farmers are cultivating officially released biofortified or nutrient-dense varieties.
disaggregationRequired: Required: sex of the farmer making the planting decision (female/male at minimum); age (youth/non-youth, youth taken as 15 to 30, stated once in Core Section 4.1); and crop, since crop is a required disaggregation alongside sex and age: trait availability and seed systems differ so much between maize and wheat that a pooled figure conceals which crop is moving. Sex and age are required because the CIMMYT register carries this indicator as age and sex disaggregated; the crop requirement is CIMMYT's own, applied on the sheet's authority. The female/male minimum rests on the register's own disaggregation rule. No CGIAR sex-disaggregation standard is named in this sheet or in the sources consulted, so none is cited for it. The youth band is 15 to 30, stated once in Core Section 4.1, and projects record date of birth or exact age so that other bands, for example a donor band of 15 to 29, can be derived later. Sex and age are recorded for the person who decides what is planted on the plot, which is not always the household head.
disaggregationRequiredForProjectType: Variety, for seed systems and deployment and breeding and varietal development projects. Those two types deliver the variety, so which of the eligible releases a farmer grew is the cut they need; the share itself is unchanged by it.
disaggregationProjectSpecific: Nutrient trait class (provitamin A, zinc, iron, protein quality); farm size class, where smallholder is defined in Annex B and the declared threshold travels with the value; seed source (own saved seed, agrodealer, project distribution, other farmers); agroecological zone; district.
unitOfObservation: Individual (the farmer), with the plot roster nested underneath.
calculationSummary: Numerator: target farmers who cultivated at least one eligible biofortified or nutrient-dense CIMMYT release on land they individually manage, during the reference cropping seasons. Denominator: all farmers in the target population assessed in the same round. Value = (numerator / denominator) x 100, applying survey weights where the design requires them. Change: the percentage-point difference between the current and baseline shares, both measured on the same population with the same instrument. Every inclusion, exclusion, missing-data and repeated-observation rule is in Eligibility criteria and missing data; none is restated here.
dataSource: Recommended DS1: farmer or household adoption survey covering the defined target population, with a plot roster identifying the variety grown. Because farmers often cannot name or misname what they grow, this realistically means the survey supported by variety identification: DNA fingerprinting of field samples against a genetic reference library, or documented seed-source records tying an eligible variety to the plot. Fallback DS2: the project M&E and seed distribution registry, acceptable only as a labelled fallback, never as the recommended source: it estimates the numerator from records of biofortified seed supplied to registered target farmers, with documented assumptions validated by spot checks. It records seed received rather than land planted, so it systematically overstates adoption: a farmer who received seed and did not plant it appears as an adopter. Where it is used, the value is labelled a distribution-based upper estimate. Fallback DS4: published national or regional adoption studies for the same crop and area, admissible for context only, since a national dataset cannot resolve a project's target population and so cannot supply the denominator. Not applicable DS3: Earth observation can map crop area but cannot tell which variety is planted, still less whether it carries a nutrient-density trait, and cannot count farmers. Not applicable DS5: crowdsourced and mobile data cannot establish variety identity reliably and cannot define the target population.
dataSourceProjectSpecific: State which source was used. If Fallback DS2 (the registry), state why an adoption survey of the target population was not feasible, which records were used, and what assumptions converted them into a farmer count. State separately whether DS4 published studies were used, and for what. DS4 produces neither the numerator nor the denominator, so its use does not make the value fallback-sourced.
collectionInstrument: Plot roster module within the farmer or household adoption survey: crop, season, plot area, farmer-reported variety name, seed source and year of seed acquisition, plus a grain or leaf sample for genotyping where variety names cannot be trusted. Respondent: the person who makes planting decisions for the plot, whose sex and age are recorded for the required disaggregations. Mode: face-to-face interview, with a plot visit where samples are taken.
collectionFrequency: With each adoption survey round: baseline and endline at minimum, and a midline every 2 to 3 years for multi-year programmes. Annually where the project M&E registry fallback is used.
reportingFrequency: Annually. Between survey rounds the latest measured value is carried forward with its year of measurement stated, and no change is claimed between a measured value and a carried-forward one.
referencePeriod: The cropping seasons falling within the reporting year, compared against the pre-intervention baseline season or year.
baselineRequired: Yes. A share on its own says little, since starting adoption levels differ by crop, country and how the target population was drawn; the indicator earns its meaning from the direction and size of change. Fallbacks where no prospective baseline exists: an earlier adoption survey round covering the same population, or a recall-based reconstruction of the pre-project season (weakest option, labelled as such). If none is feasible: monitoring only, with no change claim.
aggregationRule:
A: Pooling domain. (2) Aggregation across projects: pool Recommended-sourced values directly; a project reporting from the registry fallback is shown alongside the pooled figure with a note, never blended in, since seed received and land planted are different quantities and mixing them biases the figure upward.

B: Combination method. Pooled by summing numerators and denominators: the institutional figure is total eligible-variety cultivators divided by total target farmers across projects reporting from the Recommended source, applying survey weights where designs require them. Never average project-level percentages.

C: Levels and operations. A share is recomputed at every level from its own numerator and denominator, never averaged from the levels beneath it: a mean of project percentages weights a project of thirty equally with one of three thousand. At Farm / Plot, the plot roster establishes which eligible varieties were grown and no share is reported, since the unit of the share is the farmer and a farmer with four qualifying plots is one farmer. At project level, target farmers who grew at least one eligible variety over all target farmers assessed in the same round. At Regional / Aggregated and institutional level, the summed numerator over the summed denominator within the pooling domain of Block A, computed from farmer records rather than from project shares. Also report: the denominator itself, the number of farmers excluded under Eligibility, the share whose variety could not be identified, and the non-response share, since a share without its denominator cannot be read.

D: Never pooled. (1) Aggregation across results levels: no. This value never combines arithmetically with varieties released or disseminated at output level (KPI-O07, KPI-O06), with per-capita biofortified grain availability (KPI-OC08), or with food insecurity prevalence (KPI-I02); those levels connect through the theory of change, not by arithmetic.

E: Deduplication and coverage. (3) Double counting: de-duplicate farmers by identifier before pooling where target populations overlap, and count each farmer once per reporting year. Overlap with other register indicators is expected and legitimate: a farmer growing a CIMMYT biofortified variety is also adopting an improved input under KPI-OC16 and, where the variety is also stress-tolerant, a resilience practice under KPI-OC20. Nothing is summed across those indicators, so the same farmer may appear in each; the shares are never added.
eligibilityCriteriaMissingData: Inclusions: individually managed land only; a farmer counts once whether they grew one eligible variety or four, on one plot or several. The varieties that count are releases, in any year, meeting KPI-O07's inclusion rules for the crops and countries the project covers, and a national partner's release built on CIMMYT germplasm counts, on the same parent-or-grandparent ancestry rule used by KPI-O07, KPI-OC12 and KPI-OC14.
limitations: Supports a contribution claim only. Whether a farmer plants a biofortified variety depends on seed availability and price, extension reach, grain colour and taste preferences, and milling and market demand; CIMMYT is one contributor among many, alongside national partners releasing the same genetics under their own names.

Variety identification is the main source of measurement error. Except where the trait changes the grain's appearance, as with provitamin-A maize, nutrient density cannot be seen in the field, so self-reported variety names carry the numerator unless genotyping or a documented seed-source record backs them up.

Comparability across projects is limited by the denominator. Each project defines its target farmers, so a project targeting only farmers already receiving biofortified seed reports a high share meaning something materially different from the same share across a whole district. Compare within a project over time first.
The value is a snapshot of one year. Annual values cannot be summed into a cumulative number of adopters, and a stable share can hide churn, with as many farmers dropping the variety as taking it up.

A rise means more targeted farmers are growing these varieties, not that anyone ate more micronutrients or that nutritional status improved. The consumption and availability steps are measured separately; read this indicator with them, not ahead of them.
subMetrics: None. Sex, age, crop and nutrient trait class are disaggregations of the same share, not separately calculated metrics. Related indicators carry their own sheets: KPI-O07 (varieties released), whose inclusion rules define the eligible varieties; KPI-O06 (varieties disseminated); KPI-OC08 (per-capita biofortified grain available for consumption), which this indicator feeds; and KPI-I02 (prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity).
referenceStandardsAndLinks:
Counting rule: No normative international standard defines adoption of biofortified varieties. The counting rules on this sheet are CIMMYT's own convention, stated on CIMMYT's authority: one count per farmer per reporting year, individually managed land only, annual values never summed across years, and estimation from distribution records admitted only as a labelled fallback with validated assumptions. The smallholder threshold, where farm size class is reported, is Annex B's.

Every other source is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports; the reference list is at the end of this volume.
sheetStewardDataRoles: Data collection: project M&E team and enumerators; genotyping laboratory or service provider where used. Validation: project MEAL officer for data quality; CIMMYT breeding and seed systems teams for whether a variety meets KPI-O07's inclusion rules and for its trait. Calculation: CIMMYT MEAL unit (weighting, exclusions, pooling, de-duplication). Approval: project leader. Reporting: project MEAL focal point to the CIMMYT MEAL unit.
sourceRef: Volume 3 · Nutrition & food security — Reference sheet KPI-OC10

name: Change in per-capita staple food availability in CIMMYT intervention areas
resultsLevel: Outcome. The value is a change against a baseline in the staple food available per person in the households of the intervention area, driven by their own production, sale, storage and purchase decisions: a change in performance among beneficiaries, which is the Core's definition of an outcome. It sits at the edge of the boundary CGIAR uses, whose outcome test turns on changes in knowledge, attitudes, skills and relationships rather than in the material condition of a population. CIMMYT's own MEAL Framework definition governs the register, so the level the register records stands: Outcome, as the step feeding the food insecurity impact indicator (KPI-I02); the divergence from CGIAR's reading is handled once in the crosswalk annex.
primaryObjective: PO2 Food and nutrition security in the global south is ensured within planetary boundaries. Contributing: PO3 (Smallholder farmers and their livelihood trajectories are resilient and significantly improved).
cgiarImpactArea: Nutrition, Health & Food Security
sdgTarget: None. No SDG indicator measures per-capita food availability. The construct is an input to SDG indicator 2.1.1 (prevalence of undernourishment), whose FAO methodology derives average dietary energy consumption from food balance sheets, but 2.1.1 reports a national prevalence of insufficient consumption, not a quantity of food available in a project area. Target 2.1 (end hunger and ensure access by all people to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round) is the target this indicator serves without matching an indicator under it.
otherFrameworks: FAO food balance sheets and the FAOSTAT food supply series (kilograms per capita per year and kilocalories per capita per day) apply the same accounting identity at national scale, and are what the household-level measure is modelled on. No CGIAR standard indicator corresponds to it, and no donor reporting framework carries a per-capita food availability indicator.
definition: Measures how much staple food, in kilograms of grain equivalent, is available for human consumption per person per year in the households of a CIMMYT intervention area, and how that quantity has changed since the baseline year. Availability is a supply concept, not a consumption concept: it counts staple food that reaches the household and stays there to be eaten, whatever its origin. It follows the accounting logic of FAO food balance sheets, where food available for human consumption is what is produced plus what comes in, minus what goes out to sale, seed, animal feed, processing and losses, divided by the population.
rationale: Answers whether more staple food is reaching people in CIMMYT intervention areas, the quantity step between higher farm productivity and lower food insecurity. Yield gains can leave household food supply unchanged if the extra grain is sold, lost in storage, or offset by a smaller planted area, so availability is the check that the productivity narrative reached the plate. It serves project management, institutional reporting on food and nutrition security, and donors.
projectSpecificApplication: State which intervention districts, production year and household population the project measures, and confirm the staple basket applied is the version CIMMYT fixed centrally for the country, with endline on the version in force at baseline. Do not change the unit, the balance identity or the calculation method. If the full balance cannot be measured, use a fallback source and label the value accordingly rather than redefining the indicator here.
projectSpecificRationale: State the project decision or donor requirement this value informs. Typical use: availability that stays flat while measured yields rise points to post-harvest losses, distress sales or shrinking planted area rather than to a production problem, and triggers a review of the storage, marketing or land-allocation components.
projectTypesNotApplicable: whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no household population whose food balance could be measured
projectTypesRaw:
Breeding and varietal development; applied agronomy and farming systems; seed systems and deployment; system change and transformation; digital agriculture and AI.

Not applicable: upstream discovery science, whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no household population whose food balance could be measured.
unit: Kilograms of grain equivalent per person per year, reported per staple crop and as a total staple aggregate, with the kilocalorie conversion reported alongside, which is what makes the value comparable with FAO food supply series. The reported value is the change against baseline, as a difference in kilograms per person per year and as a percentage of the baseline value.
directionOfChange: Increase, and it carries no formal ceiling. A rising value means more staple food is available per person per year.
disaggregationRequired: Required: staple crop, plus the total staple aggregate. Crops differ in yield, storability, market role and energy density, so a pooled figure that hides its crop composition can move purely because the crop mix changed. The register carries no disaggregation for this indicator, so the staple-crop requirement is CIMMYT's own, applied on the sheet's authority. No further cut is required, consistent with the unit of observation: availability is measured for the household as a whole and cannot be attributed to individuals inside it.
disaggregationRequiredForProjectType: None. The register names a project type in none of its rows, so no cut is required by project type; the cuts above apply to every type that reports this indicator.
disaggregationProjectSpecific: Sex of household head; farm size class; agroecological zone; rural or peri-urban location; season or post-harvest quarter, where seasonal depletion is the management question.
unitOfObservation: Household
calculationSummary: Numerator: staple food available for human consumption to sampled households over the 12-month reference period, in kilograms of grain equivalent, per household as own production (harvest measured as in Sapkota et al. (2016)) plus purchases, plus food received as gifts, transfers, aid or wages in kind, plus net drawdown of opening stocks, minus quantities sold, retained for seed or animal feed, or diverted to non-food processing, minus measured or estimated storage and handling losses. Denominator: resident household members over the same period, a headcount in person-years, not adult equivalents, so a member present part of the year counts in proportion and the value stays comparable with FAO's per-capita supply figures, which use headcount; where a project needs an intake-sensitive read, the adult-equivalent figure is reported alongside with the scale named. Value = numerator / denominator, per crop and summed across the staple basket, applying survey weights; the reported figure is this value minus the baseline value. Local units, purchased flour and meal, and non-grain staples are converted to kilograms of grain equivalent, and grain equivalent to kilocalories, with every conversion factor and the food composition table named against the value; two values are comparable only where the same factors were used. Every inclusion, exclusion, missing-data and repeated-observation rule is in Eligibility criteria and missing data; none is restated here.
dataSource: Recommended DS1: household survey carrying a staple food balance module (harvest, sales, purchases, transfers, opening and closing stocks, seed and feed retention, storage losses) with objective measurement of production, that is GPS-measured plot area with crop cuts or whole-plot harvest, measured as in Sapkota et al. (2016), rather than recall alone. Frame DS1: the household roster supplies the denominator. Fallback DS3: Earth observation and geospatial products for the production component only, with gridded population data. This cannot see sales, purchases, transfers, stocks or losses, and satellite yield estimation needs ground calibration and confuses crops with similar spectral signatures, so such a value is a production-side proxy and is labelled as one. Fallback DS4: national or subnational food balance sheets and agricultural statistics (FAO food balance sheets via FAOSTAT, national crop production and household expenditure statistics), used only where the project cannot field its own survey; compiled at national level, they normally cannot resolve an intervention area, so any value is flagged as fallback-sourced. Not applicable DS2: project and partner administrative records document what was distributed or trained, not what households produced, bought, sold, stored or lost, so they cannot close the balance. Not applicable DS5: crowdsourced and mobile data cannot establish household-level quantities with the accuracy an accounting identity requires.
dataSourceProjectSpecific: State which source role was used, Recommended or Fallback (and which fallback), the reason primary collection was not feasible, and the resolution of the data used.
collectionInstrument: Staple food balance module in the household survey: plot roster with GPS area and crop cut or whole-plot harvest; disposition module covering sales, purchases, transfers, seed and feed retention, non-food processing and storage losses; stock inventory at the start and end of the period; household roster with months of residence. Respondent: the member responsible for grain storage and disposal, with the plot decision-maker for the production module. Mode: face-to-face, visiting plots and the storage structure.
collectionFrequency: Baseline and endline at minimum, with a midline every 2 to 3 years in multi-year programmes. Where a project measures more often, the survey must fall at the same point in the agricultural calendar each time.
reportingFrequency: Annually. Between measurement waves the latest measured value is carried forward with its year of measurement stated, never interpolated.
referencePeriod: The 12 months of one production and marketing year, ending after the main harvest is stored, compared against the same 12-month window in the pre-intervention baseline year.
baselineRequired: Yes. The indicator is defined as a change, so without a baseline there is no value to report. Fallbacks where no prospective baseline exists: an earlier survey round in the same area using the same staple basket, or recall-based reconstruction of the previous year's harvest, sales and purchases, labelled as such. If none is feasible: monitor the level only, with no change claim.
aggregationRule:
A: Pooling domain. (2) Aggregation across projects: pool Recommended-sourced values directly, weighting by person-years; a project that used either fallback for any component of its value is presented alongside the pooled figure with a note naming the fallback-sourced components, their source and resolution, never blended in, since a geospatial proxy and a national food balance sheet measure a different thing at a different scale.

B: Combination method. Pooled and population-weighted: the institutional figure is total available staple quantity divided by total person-years across all reporting households, applying survey weights. Never average project-level per-capita figures, since household sizes differ.

C: Levels and operations. A per-capita quantity is a ratio, recomputed at every level from its own numerator and denominator, never averaged from the levels beneath it: a mean of project per-capita figures weights a panel of two hundred person-years equally with one of twenty thousand. The reported change is recomputed the same way, as the difference between two figures each built at that level, never as a mean of project-level changes. At Household, the kilograms of grain equivalent available over that household's resident person-years, per crop and summed across the staple basket. At project level and at Regional / Aggregated, the summed available quantity over the summed person-years within the pooling domain of Block A, and the difference of that figure against the same construction in the baseline year. Also report: the person-year denominator, the number of households excluded for an incomplete balance, the centrally fixed staple basket version in force and confirmation that it is the version applied at baseline, and the per-crop figures alongside the aggregate, since a total that moved only because the crop mix changed is not a change in staple availability.

D: Never pooled. (1) Aggregation across results levels: no. This value never combines arithmetically with productivity indicators or with the food insecurity impact indicator (KPI-I02); levels connect through the theory of change as a narrative, not by arithmetic.

E: Deduplication and coverage. (3) Double counting: as a per-capita ratio rather than a count, overlap distorts the weights rather than inflating a total. Where two projects' sampling frames overlap, pool only surveys whose frames partition the domain, or re-derive the design weights for the combined sample; where neither is possible, report the project values separately. Two register overlaps must be stated whenever the value is reported: biofortified grain (KPI-OC08) counts inside this staple total, so the two values share grain and are never summed, since adding them would double-count it; the share meeting the minimum dietary energy requirement (KPI-OC07) measures consumption against a requirement, not supply, and is not an alternative expression of this value.
eligibilityCriteriaMissingData:
Inclusions: the crops in the staple basket for the country; CIMMYT fixes it centrally per country, not each project, and it is held constant across rounds; a crop is added mid-programme only at a stated version boundary, with the prior series restated on the new basket or clearly broken, never silently extended. Members resident at least one month.

Exclusions: crops grown purely for sale and not eaten in the household; food consumed away from home, which household accounting cannot capture.

Missing data: households missing any balance component are excluded from both numerator and denominator rather than imputed, since the identity requires the full set, and the excluded share is published with the value.

Repeated observations: the unit is the household-year; a household surveyed in successive years contributes one value per reference year, and where a household is re-contacted within one round only the first complete interview counts.
limitations: Supports a contribution claim only. Staple availability responds to rainfall, prices, market access, land allocation and off-farm income as much as to anything CIMMYT introduces.

Availability is not consumption and not nutrition. It counts staple quantity entering the household, so it cannot show who inside the household eats it, whether diets are diverse, or whether anyone's energy requirement is met; a rise concentrated in one cereal can coincide with a narrower diet.

Measurement error runs on both sides of the balance. Storage losses, seed and feed retention and small informal sales are the weakest recalled quantities, local unit conversions add error, and the denominator depends on an accurate roster with seasonal migration handled consistently.

Comparability is limited to like with like: only where the staple basket, the point in the agricultural calendar and the source role match. A production-side geospatial proxy is not comparable with a fully measured household balance.

A rise means more staple grain was available per person in the surveyed households that year, not that CIMMYT caused it, not that food insecurity fell, and not that nutrition improved. Read it with the food insecurity and dietary adequacy indicators.
subMetrics: None. Per-crop figures are disaggregations of the same calculation, and the balance components (production, sales, purchases, transfers, stocks, losses) are inputs to the formula, not indicators in their own right. Related indicators carry their own sheets: KPI-OC08 (per-capita biofortified grain available), KPI-OC07 (share meeting the minimum dietary energy requirement), and KPI-I02 (prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity), to which this indicator rolls up.
referenceStandardsAndLinks: Every other source is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports; the reference list is at the end of this volume.
sheetStewardDataRoles: Data collection: project M&E team and enumerators (plot measurement, crop cuts, disposition and stock modules, household roster). Validation: project MEAL officer for survey data quality and balance-identity consistency checks. Calculation: CIMMYT MEAL unit (conversion factors, weighting, exclusions, pooling, de-duplication). Approval: project leader. Reporting: project MEAL focal point to the CIMMYT MEAL unit.
sourceRef: Volume 3 · Nutrition & food security — Reference sheet KPI-OC13

name: Percentage of CIMMYT innovations that reach nutritionally vulnerable populations
resultsLevel: Outcome, as recorded in the register. CIMMYT's own MEAL Framework definition governs the register, so the level the register records stands. CGIAR's control-and-externality test would read documented reach, a property of how CIMMYT and its partners deliver, as an output; that divergence is recorded as a comparison and handled once in the crosswalk annex rather than re-argued here.
primaryObjective: PO2 Food and nutrition security in the global south is ensured within planetary boundaries. Contributing: PO3 (Smallholder farmers and their livelihood trajectories are resilient and significantly improved).
cgiarImpactArea: Nutrition, Health & Food Security
sdgTarget: None. The indicator serves SDG target 2.2 (end all forms of malnutrition, including the agreed targets on stunting and wasting in children under five, and address the nutritional needs of adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women, and older persons), and takes its vulnerable-group list from that wording. No official SDG indicator corresponds: those under target 2.2 measure nutritional status in the population (2.2.1 stunting, 2.2.2 wasting and overweight, 2.2.3 anaemia in women aged 15 to 49), whereas this one measures the composition of an institution's delivery portfolio.
otherFrameworks: CGIAR Results Framework: the outcome result category Innovation use, whose standard indicators count people using an innovation, disaggregated by gender, and innovations being used. This indicator uses the same innovation inventory but asks who was reached rather than how many. CGIAR innovation portfolio management (Innovation Packages and Scaling Readiness), which maintains the innovation records the denominator is built from.
definition: The share of the innovations CIMMYT disseminated in the reporting year with documented evidence of reaching people who are nutritionally vulnerable. Numerator: innovations with documented reach to at least one such group. Denominator: all innovations disseminated in the same year and scope. An innovation is CGIAR's innovation-development and innovation-use construct, sourced in Other frameworks. "Nutritionally vulnerable" is CIMMYT's own convention for this indicator: SDG target 2.2's groups plus food-insecure households, listed in Eligibility criteria and missing data. The indicator measures equity of reach across the portfolio, not the size of the population reached and not any change in nutritional status.
rationale: Answers whether CIMMYT's innovations are reaching the people who most need better nutrition, or only the farmers who are easiest to reach. Institutional reporting and donors use it as the equity check on the nutrition portfolio: a rising count of disseminated innovations says nothing about who received them, and this share supplies that missing half. Project management uses it to decide whether delivery channels and partner selection need to change.
projectSpecificApplication: State which innovations fall inside the project's portfolio for the reporting year, the countries and delivery channels through which they were disseminated, and which vulnerability criteria the project applied. Do not change the numerator and denominator construction, the innovation definition, or the vulnerability criteria. Where the project cannot characterise who was reached, report the count of innovations with no reach evidence alongside the value and raise the gap with the MEAL focal point.
projectSpecificRationale: State the project decision or donor commitment this share informs: for example a donor requirement to evidence targeting of nutritionally vulnerable groups, or a decision to add community-based or women-focused delivery channels if the share stays low while dissemination rises.
projectTypesNotApplicable: whose outputs have not been disseminated to end users and so enter neither term of the share
projectTypesRaw:
Breeding and varietal development; applied agronomy and farming systems; seed systems and deployment; system change and transformation; digital agriculture and AI.

Not applicable: upstream discovery science, whose outputs have not been disseminated to end users and so enter neither term of the share.
unit: Percentage of disseminated innovations
directionOfChange: Increase. A rising value means a larger share of disseminated innovations reached nutritionally vulnerable populations.
disaggregationRequired: Innovation type and vulnerable-group category are required disaggregations: innovation type (following the CGIAR innovation categories used in CIMMYT's innovation records) and vulnerable-group category reached (children under five, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women, older persons, food-insecure households). The register records no required disaggregation for this indicator, so both cuts are CIMMYT's own, applied on the sheet's authority: without innovation type the share cannot be read against its own portfolio, and the vulnerable-group category must already be established to apply the numerator test.
disaggregationRequiredForProjectType: None. The register names a project type in none of its rows, so no cut is required by project type; the cuts above apply to every type that reports this indicator.
disaggregationProjectSpecific: Country or subnational delivery area; delivery channel (public extension, seed company or agrodealer, farmer organisation, humanitarian or social protection programme, school or health platform); crop and trait class; sex of the person or household head reached.
unitOfObservation: Result object: the innovation, identified by a unique innovation identifier, counted from CIMMYT's own records under the Core's result object value. The reach determination for each innovation rests on individual or household-level evidence collected under the instrument above.
calculationSummary: Numerator: innovations disseminated in the reporting year with documented evidence that at least one nutritionally vulnerable group, per the definition above, was among those reached. On the Recommended route the evidence threshold is documented delivery to identified individuals or households in a vulnerable category: delivery into an area where vulnerable people live does not meet it, since it shows where an innovation went, not who received it. Denominator: all CIMMYT innovations disseminated in the same year and scope, not only the nutrition-relevant ones, since restricting the denominator would answer a much narrower question while looking like the broader one. Value = (numerator / denominator) x 100. Every inclusion, exclusion, missing-data and repeated-observation rule is in Eligibility criteria and missing data; none is restated here.
dataSource: Recommended DS2: CIMMYT's own innovation records and the dissemination, seed distribution and partner delivery records attached to them, authoritative for the denominator, not the subset reported into CGIAR's performance system, which is filtered by that system's own reporting rules and would make the denominator depend on what CIMMYT chose to report upward. Only this source can establish the denominator, an inventory of the institution's own innovations. Recommended DS1: the beneficiary or household survey that characterises who was reached, carrying an age, sex and life-stage screen for the groups in the definition and, where food insecurity is the criterion, a validated food security module. DS1 supplies the numerator, since DS2 alone can rarely establish vulnerability. Fallback DS4: subnational nutrition and food security statistics (demographic and health surveys, national nutrition surveys, published SDG 2.2 series) used to classify the delivery area rather than the people reached, only where no beneficiary characterisation exists, and always flagged as fallback-sourced, because area-level prevalence does not establish that the individuals reached were vulnerable. Fallback DS3: geospatial and Earth observation data, used only to delimit the delivery area then matched to those statistics; it locates delivery and cannot observe who received anything, so it is never sufficient alone. Not applicable DS5: crowdsourced and other non-traditional data can establish neither an institutional innovation inventory nor a person's nutritional vulnerability status to a reportable standard.
dataSourceProjectSpecific: State which route each innovation's reach evidence rests on, Recommended or Fallback; name the innovations on the Fallback, whose reach was classified by delivery area only, and state how many remained without any reach evidence.
collectionInstrument: Beneficiary or household survey module recording, for each recipient, whether the recipient belongs to one of the vulnerable groups in Eligibility criteria and missing data and, where food insecurity is the criterion, the recipient household's status on a validated food security module. Respondent: the household member who received the innovation, or the adult responsible for food preparation. Mode: face-to-face or phone interview, administered by the project or its delivery partner.
collectionFrequency: Annually, compiled at year end from innovation and dissemination records with the reach evidence available for that year; where that evidence comes from a periodic survey, use the round nearest the dissemination year and state its date.
reportingFrequency: Annually. Because the denominator in a single project or year can be small, report the numerator and denominator counts alongside the percentage, and at institutional level a three-year pooled figure, the summed numerators of the three years over their summed denominators, so an innovation disseminated in more than one of the three years counts in each.
referencePeriod: The reporting year in which dissemination occurred, on the same calendar or fiscal basis as CIMMYT's innovation reporting. Reach evidence may be collected later but is attributed to the year of dissemination.
baselineRequired: Yes, since a single year's share is only interpretable against a starting point. The denominator can normally be recomputed retrospectively from dissemination records; the constraint is the reach evidence, rarely available for past years. Where no prospective baseline exists: set the first year with beneficiary-level evidence as the baseline. If no fallback is feasible: monitoring only, with no change claims.
aggregationRule:
A: Pooling domain. (2) Aggregation across projects: pool the innovations whose reach is evidenced at beneficiary level (Recommended); an innovation classified only by delivery area (Fallback) is reported alongside the pooled figure with a note naming it, not blended in, since that is a weaker claim about the same variable; the same project's beneficiary-evidenced innovations stay in the pool.

B: Combination method. Pool as one ratio: de-duplicate innovations by unique identifier, then sum numerators and sum denominators across projects and countries and divide. Never average project-level percentages, which gives a project with three innovations the same weight as one with thirty.

C: Levels and operations. A share is recomputed at every level from its own numerator and denominator, never averaged from the levels beneath it. The measurement levels do not apply to this one: the unit is the innovation, and an innovation has no plot and no household, so the levels here are reporting levels. At project level, that project's innovations with documented reach to at least one nutritionally vulnerable group, over its innovations disseminated in the same year and scope. At institutional level, both terms are recomputed from the de-duplicated innovation inventory rather than summed across projects, since one innovation disseminated by three projects is one innovation in the numerator and one in the denominator alike, and summing would inflate both terms unequally. Also report: both counts rather than the percentage alone, the number of innovations excluded for want of any reach evidence, and the number of innovations reported alongside because their reach rests on delivery-area classification.

D: Never pooled. (1) Aggregation across results levels: no. This share does not combine arithmetically with the output counts it draws on (KPI-O06, biofortified varieties disseminated; KPI-O08, people reached with nutrition-sensitive information) or with the outcome and impact indicators in the pathway (KPI-OC10; KPI-I02). They connect through the theory of change, not through arithmetic.

E: Deduplication and coverage. (3) Double counting: the same innovation is frequently disseminated by several projects and countries, so de-duplicate by unique innovation identifier before pooling, in numerator and denominator alike. Overlap runs the other way too: these innovations are also counted in KPI-O06 and the innovation-pathway indicators, so the figures must never be summed into a portfolio total. Where identifiers cannot be matched across reporting units, label the pooled figure an upper estimate.
eligibilityCriteriaMissingData:
Inclusion: the nutritionally vulnerable groups are children under five, adolescent girls, pregnant and lactating women, older persons, and households classified as food insecure; the food-insecurity extension is CIMMYT's own and is stated as such, because an agricultural organisation reaching a food-insecure household is the case the SDG groups alone would miss. Innovations that reached end users through active distribution or delivery in the reporting year, including biofortified varieties, each counted as CIMMYT's innovation records identify it.

Exclusion: innovations developed, validated or released but not yet disseminated (KPI-O01, KPI-O02, KPI-OC02); innovations disseminated in an earlier year with no new delivery in this one.

Missing data: an innovation whose reached population cannot be characterised at beneficiary level or, on the Fallback DS4 route, by delivery area is excluded from both numerator and denominator, never counted as not reaching vulnerable groups, and the excluded count is reported with the value. An innovation classified only by delivery area on the Fallback DS4 route is flagged fallback-sourced, leaves both terms of the share at every level and is reported alongside it; an innovation with beneficiary-level evidence from any project is Recommended-sourced.

Repeated observations: one count per innovation, whether it reached several groups, countries or channels, or was disseminated by more than one project.
limitations: Counts innovations, not people. Every innovation carries equal weight, so one that reached a handful of vulnerable households scores the same as one that reached hundreds of thousands. The share describes the portfolio, not the population, and must be read next to the reach counts in KPI-O08 and the adoption share in KPI-OC10.

Two definitional choices set the value before any data is collected: what counts as an innovation in the denominator, and what counts as reaching a vulnerable group. A loose reading, any innovation delivered anywhere a vulnerable group lives, scores near 100 percent and carries no information; a strict reading, documented delivery to identified vulnerable individuals, scores lower, but because one qualifying recipient is enough, an innovation delivered to many recipients still almost always qualifies where vulnerable groups are common among them. Values built on different readings are not comparable, so the reading must be stated with every figure.

Reach is neither use nor nutritional benefit. CGIAR's own review of its standard indicators found that indicators framed around people benefiting from innovations leave the nature and degree of benefit unspecified, and warned against extrapolating benefits from reach or use figures.

Evidence availability, not targeting performance, drives much of the year-to-year movement. Projects with a survey can demonstrate reach; projects without one cannot, and their innovations drop out of the calculation. Always report how many were excluded for lack of evidence.

A rise means a larger share of the year's disseminated innovations had documented reach to nutritionally vulnerable groups. It does not mean nutritional status improved, or that CIMMYT caused any improvement that did occur.
subMetrics: None. The splits by vulnerable-group category and innovation type are disaggregations of one numerator, not separately calculated metrics. Related sheets: KPI-O06 (biofortified or nutrient-dense varieties disseminated), part of the denominator; KPI-O08 (people reached with nutrition-sensitive information or training); KPI-OC10 (farmers cultivating biofortified varieties); KPI-I02 (prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity), the pathway's impact destination.
referenceStandardsAndLinks: Every other source is cited inline at the point of the claim it supports; the reference list is at the end of this volume.
sheetStewardDataRoles: Data collection: project M&E team and delivery partners (dissemination records); project enumerators (beneficiary survey). Validation: project MEAL officer, confirming for each innovation in the numerator that the reach evidence names a vulnerable group under the institutional criteria. Calculation: CIMMYT MEAL unit, per the Calculation method above, after de-duplicating the innovation list. Approval: project team lead, with the nutrition or GEYSI technical lead confirming the vulnerability classification. Reporting: project MEAL focal point to the CIMMYT MEAL unit.
sourceRef: Volume 3 · Nutrition & food security — Reference sheet KPI-OC15

name: Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity among households in CIMMYT intervention areas, based on the Food Insecurity Experience Scale (FIES)
resultsLevel: Impact, as recorded in the register. Household food insecurity is the longer-term, population-level change that all seven of the pathway's outcomes (KPI-OC06 to KPI-OC10, KPI-OC13 and KPI-OC15) contribute to, neither a delivered result nor a change among the partners the work engages. CGIAR likewise files food security among its impact-level standard indicators.
indicatorScope: Mission. Measures a condition experienced by households in CIMMYT intervention areas, reached through project implementation, so the sheet carries the project-specific layer.
domain: Cross-cutting / Common, as recorded in the register.
primaryObjective: PO2 Food and nutrition security in the global south is ensured within planetary boundaries. One primary objective only; the register lists PO2 first, its convention for the primary. Contributing, contribution only: PO3 (smallholder farmers and their livelihood trajectories are resilient and significantly improved), since a household's ability to access food follows from the income, productivity and resilience of its farming livelihood.
cgiarImpactArea: Nutrition, Health & Food Security.
sdgTarget: SDG indicator 2.1.2 (prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity in the population, based on FIES), under target 2.1 (end hunger and ensure access by all people to safe, nutritious and sufficient food all year round). Custodian: FAO. One difference must be stated whenever a value is presented as an SDG 2.1.2 contribution: the official indicator is a prevalence among individuals, this one, as the register defines it, a prevalence among households. They are not interchangeable; the conversion is under Eligibility criteria and missing data.
otherFrameworks: FAO Voices of the Hungry, the global monitoring programme that established and maintains the scale. CGIAR Common Results Framework: partial correspondence with the impact-level standard indicator "number of people benefiting from relevant CGIAR innovations" under Nutrition, Health and Food Security. The correspondence is directional, not arithmetic: that indicator is a beneficiary headcount, this one a prevalence rate, and neither can be derived from the other.
definition: The percentage of households in CIMMYT intervention areas that experienced food insecurity at moderate or severe levels during the 12 months before data collection. Severity of food insecurity is a latent trait, measured through the experiences people report. It is measured with the Food Insecurity Experience Scale, the standard FAO established by applying the scale in more than 140 countries since 2014. Each household's eight yes or no answers are analysed with a Rasch model (a one-parameter logistic item response model) that places the household on a continuous severity scale and gives the probability it falls in the moderate or severe category. Those probabilities, not a headcount of affirmative answers, produce the prevalence.
rationale: Answers whether households in CIMMYT intervention areas are less often unable to access enough food over time: the end condition CIMMYT's food and nutrition security work exists to change. Because the scale is an FAO global standard calibrated to a single reference scale, values are comparable across countries and rounds and feed directly into institutional, CGIAR and donor reporting.
projectSpecificApplication: State this project's surveyed population, geographic boundary and survey timing. The institutional definition, the FIES module, the unit and the calculation method stay unchanged. Example: prevalence among smallholder households in the project's zone of influence, measured at its baseline and endline rounds. If applying the indicator as defined is not feasible in this project's context, raise it with the MEAL focal point rather than redefining it here.
projectSpecificRationale: State the project decision, donor requirement or local reporting need served. Example: the donor requires a food security status measure for the zone of influence, and a rising severe insecurity rate during implementation triggers a review of the food access or transfer components paired with the agricultural intervention.
projectTypesNotApplicable: whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no intervention-area household population to sample
projectTypesRaw:
Breeding and varietal development; applied agronomy and farming systems; seed systems and deployment; system change and transformation; digital agriculture and AI.

Not applicable: upstream discovery science, whose work is laboratory and controlled-environment research with no intervention-area household population to sample.
unit: Percentage of households: households stay the register's unit, with the individual prevalence derived and reported alongside where a project's data supports it, since that is what SDG 2.1.2 and donor reporting need.
directionOfChange: Decrease. A falling value means fewer households are experiencing moderate or severe food insecurity.
disaggregationRequired: Required: the four gendered household types, CIMMYT's own convention for this indicator: male and female adults; adult female no adult male; adult male no adult female; child no adults. This replaces sex of the household head, which is a reported social role rather than an observed fact and is applied inconsistently between enumerators, whereas household composition is observable. No global-standard household typology exists to adopt: the FAO global FIES series samples individuals and disaggregates by sex of respondent, so a household-unit indicator needs its own convention, and this four-type classification is the one CIMMYT applies. The register's Disaggregation cell attributes the four categories to FIES, which does not define them. Required in addition, where at least 30 households fall in the severe category: severity level (moderate or severe; severe), because the headline value combines two classes that FAO and the SDG series report separately; below that count a severe-only percentage can move between rounds with no real change behind it.
disaggregationRequiredForProjectType: None. The register names a project type in none of its rows, so no cut is required by project type; the cuts above apply to every type that reports this indicator.
disaggregationProjectSpecific: Age of the household head (register, optional); agroecological zone; rural or urban location; district or administrative unit; season of interview; farm size class; crop or farming system.
unitOfObservation: Household
calculationSummary: Numerator: the sum, across sampled households, of each household's estimated probability of being moderately or severely food insecure, multiplied by its survey weight. The probability comes from a Rasch model fitted to the eight FIES items and calibrated to the FAO global reference scale, not from a raw count of affirmative answers. Denominator: the weighted total of all sampled households with a valid FIES record. Value = (numerator / denominator) x 100. Calibration: equate the local scale to the FAO global reference scale before applying the thresholds; FAO requires at least four of the eight items to be common between the scales. Moderate or severe begins at the severity of the fifth item ("ate less than you thought you should"), severe at the eighth ("went a whole day without eating"). Every inclusion, exclusion, missing-data and repeated-observation rule is in Eligibility criteria and missing data; none is restated here.
dataSource: Recommended, DS1 (Censuses and surveys): a population-based household survey in the intervention area carrying the 8-item FIES module, sampled to represent the intervention-area household population, with the sampling frame and the area boundary fixed before the round and held constant across rounds. Frame DS2 (Administrative and registry data): project records supplying the intervention-area boundary and the sampling frame; these frame the estimate but never produce the value. Fallback, DS4 (Secondary and international databases): national or subnational FIES rounds covering the intervention area, household-referenced as this indicator is, used only where the project cannot field its own survey. Prefer the most geographically resolved round available and flag the value as fallback-sourced: a national prevalence attributed to an intervention area is a weak substitute, not an equivalent. Not applicable, DS3 (Geospatial and Earth observation): the condition is an experience reported by a respondent and has no signature observable from satellite or aerial data. Not applicable, DS5 (Citizen-generated and other non-traditional data): the estimate needs a probability sample and a fixed eight-item module; self-selected responses satisfy neither and would bias the prevalence in an unknown direction.
